questions.q: In 1492, Christopher Columbus sailed west on a voyage paid for by the rulers of which country?
questions.explain: King Ferdinand and Queen Isabella of Spain sponsored Columbus's 1492 voyage across the Atlantic.

questions.q: What were the names of the three ships Columbus sailed in 1492?
questions.explain: Columbus crossed the Atlantic in 1492 with the Nina, the Pinta and the Santa Maria.

questions.q: When Columbus sailed west in 1492, which region was he trying to reach?
questions.explain: Columbus hoped to reach the riches of Asia, the 'Indies,' by sailing west, and instead reached the Caribbean.

questions.q: The Americas are named after which Italian explorer?
questions.explain: A 1507 map used the name 'America' for the new lands, after Amerigo Vespucci, who argued they were a new continent.

questions.q: Where did Columbus first make landfall in October 1492?
questions.explain: Columbus first landed on an island in the Bahamas that he named San Salvador, then sailed on to Cuba and Hispaniola.

questions.q: Which Spanish explorer searched Florida in 1513 and is linked by legend to a Fountain of Youth?
questions.explain: Juan Ponce de Leon led the first known Spanish expedition to Florida in 1513; the Fountain of Youth story grew up around him later.

questions.q: Which Spanish conquistador conquered the Aztec Empire in Mexico?
questions.explain: Hernan Cortes and his allies captured the Aztec capital, Tenochtitlan, in 1521.

questions.q: The Spanish conquistador Francisco Pizarro conquered which empire in South America?
questions.explain: Pizarro began his conquest of the Inca Empire, centered in the Andes of Peru, in 1532.

questions.q: Founded by Spain in 1565, which is the oldest continuously settled European-founded city in the continental United States?
questions.explain: Spain founded St. Augustine in Florida in 1565, more than 40 years before Jamestown.

questions.q: What do historians call the transfer of plants, animals and diseases between the Americas and Europe after 1492?
questions.explain: The Columbian Exchange brought corn and potatoes to Europe and horses, cattle and deadly diseases to the Americas.

questions.q: Which disease brought by Europeans caused the most deaths among Native Americans?
questions.explain: Native Americans had no immunity to smallpox, and epidemics killed a huge share of many Native populations.

questions.q: Corn, first grown in the Americas, is also known by what name?
questions.explain: Native peoples in Mexico domesticated maize, or corn, thousands of years ago; it spread worldwide after 1492.

questions.q: English settlers on Roanoke Island vanished by 1590. What nickname has the settlement had ever since?
questions.explain: When supply ships returned to Roanoke in 1590, the colonists were gone, and their fate remains a mystery.

questions.q: The name Virginia honored which English monarch, known as the Virgin Queen?
questions.explain: Virginia was named in honor of Queen Elizabeth I, the 'Virgin Queen,' who never married.

questions.q: Which Norse explorer reached North America around the year 1000, long before Columbus?
questions.explain: Leif Erikson and other Norse sailors reached Newfoundland around 1000; a Norse site survives at L'Anse aux Meadows.

questions.q: Whose expedition was the first to sail all the way around the world, from 1519 to 1522?
questions.explain: Magellan died in the Philippines, but his crew completed the first trip around the globe in 1522.

questions.q: The Haudenosaunee, or Iroquois Confederacy, united several Native nations in what is now which state?
questions.explain: The Iroquois Confederacy joined the Mohawk, Oneida, Onondaga, Cayuga and Seneca (later the Tuscarora) in present-day New York.

questions.q: Spain's reasons for exploring the Americas are often summed up in which three words?
questions.explain: Spanish explorers sought to spread Christianity, find riches and win fame, often summed up as God, gold and glory.

questions.q: Jamestown, the first lasting English colony, was founded in what present-day state?
questions.explain: The Virginia Company founded Jamestown in 1607 near the Chesapeake Bay in Virginia.

questions.q: Which daughter of the Powhatan leader is linked to John Smith and later married John Rolfe?
questions.explain: Pocahontas married colonist John Rolfe in 1614 and traveled to England, where she died in 1617.

questions.q: Which cash crop saved the struggling Jamestown colony and made Virginia rich?
questions.explain: John Rolfe began growing a sweet tobacco around 1612, and it became Virginia's main export to England.

questions.q: On what ship did the Pilgrims sail to America in 1620?
questions.explain: The Mayflower carried about 100 Pilgrims and other passengers across the Atlantic in 1620.

questions.q: Which colony did the Pilgrims found in 1620?
questions.explain: The Pilgrims founded Plymouth Colony in present-day Massachusetts in late 1620.

questions.q: Plymouth, the colony the Pilgrims founded, is in which present-day state?
questions.explain: Plymouth Colony was on Cape Cod Bay; it was merged into Massachusetts in 1691.

questions.q: Before leaving their ship in 1620, the Pilgrims signed an agreement to govern themselves. What is it called?
questions.explain: The Mayflower Compact, signed in November 1620, was an early example of self-government in the colonies.

questions.q: Which Patuxet man, who spoke English, helped the Pilgrims learn to plant corn?
questions.explain: Squanto (Tisquantum) had been kidnapped to Europe and learned English, and he helped Plymouth survive in 1621.

questions.q: The Pilgrims and the Wampanoag shared a harvest feast in 1621. That event is remembered today as the first what?
questions.explain: The 1621 harvest feast at Plymouth is remembered as the first Thanksgiving, which became a national holiday in 1863.

questions.q: The Pilgrims were Separatists who broke away from which church?
questions.explain: The Pilgrims thought the Church of England could not be reformed, so they separated from it and later left England.

questions.q: Which religious group founded the Massachusetts Bay Colony around Boston in 1630?
questions.explain: Puritans led by John Winthrop founded Massachusetts Bay in 1630, hoping to build a model Christian community.

questions.q: Puritan leader John Winthrop said the new colony would be like a 'city upon a' what, watched by all?
questions.explain: Winthrop's 1630 sermon said the colony would be 'as a city upon a hill,' a phrase later presidents quoted.

questions.q: Which religious group, led by William Penn, founded Pennsylvania?
questions.explain: William Penn, a Quaker, founded Pennsylvania in 1681 as a colony offering religious freedom.

questions.q: Which Pennsylvania city, founded by William Penn, has a name meaning 'city of brotherly love'?
questions.explain: Penn chose a Greek name for Philadelphia: philos means love and adelphos means brother.

questions.q: Lord Baltimore founded Maryland in 1634 as a safe home for which religious group?
questions.explain: Maryland was founded as a refuge for English Catholics, and its 1649 Toleration Act protected Christians of many kinds.

questions.q: Who founded Rhode Island after being banished from Massachusetts for his religious views?
questions.explain: Roger Williams founded Providence in 1636, and Rhode Island became known for religious freedom.

questions.q: Before the English took over in 1664, New York City was a Dutch town called what?
questions.explain: The Dutch founded New Amsterdam on Manhattan Island; the English renamed it New York in 1664.

questions.q: Which was the last of the original 13 colonies to be founded, chartered in 1732?
questions.explain: Georgia was chartered in 1732 and first settled at Savannah in 1733 under James Oglethorpe, as a buffer against Spanish Florida.

questions.q: How many British colonies joined together to declare independence in 1776?
questions.explain: The 13 colonies stretched along the Atlantic coast from New Hampshire to Georgia.

questions.q: In 1692, a series of famous witch trials took place in which Massachusetts town?
questions.explain: The Salem witch trials of 1692 led to the execution of 20 people accused of witchcraft.

questions.q: Meeting in 1619, what was the first elected lawmaking assembly in the English colonies?
questions.explain: Virginia's House of Burgesses first met at Jamestown in 1619, the start of representative government in English America.

questions.q: In 1619, the first recorded Africans in English mainland North America arrived in which colony?
questions.explain: In 1619, about 20 Africans were brought to Point Comfort in Virginia, the first recorded in English mainland North America.

questions.q: Which English captain led Jamestown in 1608 and ruled that colonists who did not work would not eat?
questions.explain: Captain John Smith's strict leadership helped Jamestown survive its early years.

questions.q: What was the name of the popular yearly almanac Benjamin Franklin published starting in 1732?
questions.explain: Poor Richard's Almanack was full of sayings like 'Early to bed and early to rise makes a man healthy, wealthy, and wise.'

questions.q: Benjamin Franklin is famous for flying what during a thunderstorm to show that lightning is electricity?
questions.explain: Franklin's 1752 kite experiment helped show lightning is electrical; he also invented the lightning rod.

questions.q: Benjamin Franklin's 1754 'Join, or Die' cartoon showed which animal cut into pieces?
questions.explain: The cartoon showed a snake cut into pieces labeled with colony names to urge the colonies to unite.

questions.q: What is the name of the wave of religious revival that swept the colonies in the 1730s and 1740s?
questions.explain: Preachers like Jonathan Edwards and George Whitefield led the Great Awakening, drawing huge crowds.

questions.q: In the southern colonies, large farms that relied on enslaved labor were called what?
questions.explain: Southern plantations grew crops such as tobacco, rice and indigo using the labor of enslaved Africans.

questions.q: With thick forests and good harbors, many New England colonists worked in fishing and which industry?
questions.explain: New England's forests supplied timber for ships, and its ports became centers of fishing, trade and shipbuilding.

questions.q: Spanish religious settlements in Texas and California, such as the Alamo, were called what?
questions.explain: Spanish missions were run by priests who tried to convert Native peoples to Catholicism.

questions.q: The French and Indian War, which began in 1754, was fought mainly between Britain and which country?
questions.explain: Britain and France fought for control of North America, with Native allies on both sides.

questions.q: Which young Virginia officer fought in the first clashes of the French and Indian War in 1754?
questions.explain: Washington, then 22, led Virginia troops in the Ohio Valley, where the war began.

questions.q: What did Britain gain when the French and Indian War ended in 1763?
options: Louisiana and the city of New Orleans
The Caribbean islands of Haiti and Cuba
Canada and French land east of the Mississippi
questions.explain: The 1763 Treaty of Paris gave Britain Canada and French land east of the Mississippi; Spain gave Britain Florida but kept Cuba.

questions.q: The Proclamation of 1763 banned colonists from settling west of which mountain range?
questions.explain: Britain drew the Proclamation Line along the Appalachians to reduce conflict with Native nations, angering colonists.

questions.q: The Stamp Act of 1765 placed a tax on what?
questions.explain: The Stamp Act taxed printed paper like newspapers, legal papers and playing cards, and colonists protested it fiercely.

questions.q: What did colonists mean when they protested 'no taxation without representation'?
options: They wanted lower taxes on cotton
They refused to pay any taxes ever
They wanted the king to be elected
They had no members in Parliament
questions.explain: Colonists argued that only their own elected assemblies could tax them, since they had no members in Parliament.

questions.q: In the 1770 Boston Massacre, British soldiers fired into what?
questions.explain: On March 5, 1770, soldiers fired into a crowd in Boston, killing five colonists.

questions.q: Which sailor of African and Native American descent was killed in the Boston Massacre?
questions.explain: Crispus Attucks is often called the first person killed in the American Revolution.

questions.q: In December 1773, protesters dumped chests of tea into the harbor of which city?
questions.explain: In the Boston Tea Party, colonists threw 342 chests of British East India Company tea into Boston Harbor.

questions.q: During the Boston Tea Party, many of the protesters disguised themselves as whom?
questions.explain: Many Boston Tea Party participants dressed loosely as Mohawk Indians to hide who they were.

questions.q: What were the Intolerable Acts of 1774?
questions.explain: After the Boston Tea Party, Parliament closed Boston's port and cut back self-rule in Massachusetts; colonists called these laws intolerable.

questions.q: Which Boston patriot helped lead the Sons of Liberty against British taxes?
questions.explain: Samuel Adams organized protests in Boston and helped plan the Boston Tea Party.

questions.q: On his famous 1775 ride, Paul Revere warned colonists that whose troops were coming?
questions.explain: On April 18, 1775, Paul Revere rode to warn that British regulars were marching toward Lexington and Concord.

questions.q: The signal 'one if by land, two if by sea' was shown with lanterns in which Boston church?
questions.explain: Two lanterns hung in the steeple of the Old North Church signaled the British were crossing by water.

questions.q: What was Paul Revere's trade?
questions.explain: Paul Revere was a Boston silversmith and engraver who also made a famous print of the Boston Massacre.

questions.q: Where were the first battles of the American Revolution fought in April 1775?
questions.explain: Fighting at Lexington and Concord, Massachusetts, on April 19, 1775, began the Revolutionary War.

questions.q: What were colonial militiamen who could be ready to fight on very short notice called?
questions.explain: Minutemen were trained to be ready at a minute's warning, and they fought at Lexington and Concord.

questions.q: British soldiers in the Revolution were often called what, because of their uniforms?
questions.explain: British soldiers wore bright red wool coats, so Americans called them redcoats.

questions.q: What name was given to the German soldiers Britain hired to fight in the Revolution?
questions.explain: Many of the German soldiers came from Hesse-Kassel, so Americans called them all Hessians.

questions.q: The 1775 Battle of Bunker Hill was fought just outside which city?
questions.explain: The Battle of Bunker Hill, fought mostly on nearby Breed's Hill in June 1775, was part of the siege of Boston.

questions.q: Who did the Continental Congress choose to command the Continental Army in 1775?
questions.explain: Congress named George Washington commander in chief in June 1775, and he led the army for the whole war.

questions.q: Which 1776 pamphlet by Thomas Paine persuaded many colonists to support independence?
questions.explain: Common Sense was one of the best-selling pamphlets of its time, read and shared across the colonies, and it argued plainly for independence.

questions.q: Who was the main author of the Declaration of Independence?
questions.explain: Thomas Jefferson wrote the first draft in June 1776; Adams, Franklin and Congress made changes.

questions.q: On what date did the Continental Congress adopt the Declaration of Independence?
questions.explain: Congress voted for independence on July 2, 1776, and adopted the Declaration's final wording on July 4.

questions.q: The words 'all men are created equal' come from which founding document?
questions.explain: The Declaration's second paragraph states that all men are created equal and have rights that cannot be taken away.

questions.q: The Declaration of Independence lists rights to 'Life, Liberty and the pursuit of' what?
questions.explain: Jefferson wrote that people have unalienable rights to 'Life, Liberty and the pursuit of Happiness.'

questions.q: Which delegate signed the Declaration of Independence with the largest, best-known signature?
questions.explain: John Hancock, president of Congress, signed first and large; 'John Hancock' now means a signature.

questions.q: The Declaration of Independence listed complaints against which British king?
questions.explain: King George III ruled Britain throughout the American Revolution.

questions.q: In which Philadelphia building were the Declaration of Independence and the Constitution signed?
questions.explain: Independence Hall, then the Pennsylvania State House, hosted the Second Continental Congress and the 1787 Convention.

questions.q: The Liberty Bell is famous for which flaw?
questions.explain: The bell cracked, was recast, and later developed the famous crack that left it unable to ring.

questions.q: According to a popular legend, who sewed the first American flag?
questions.explain: Betsy Ross was a Philadelphia upholsterer; historians have found no proof for the story, but the legend is widely known.

questions.q: The first official U.S. flag, adopted in 1777, had how many stars?
questions.explain: The Flag Act of 1777 called for 13 stripes and 13 stars, one for each state.

questions.q: On Christmas night 1776, George Washington crossed which river to make a surprise attack on Trenton?
questions.explain: Washington crossed the icy Delaware River and defeated Hessian troops at Trenton, New Jersey, on December 26, 1776.

questions.q: Which 1777 battle is called the turning point of the Revolution because it convinced France to join the war?
questions.explain: The American victory at Saratoga, New York, led France to sign an alliance with the United States in 1778.

questions.q: Where did Washington's army spend the harsh winter of 1777-1778?
questions.explain: About 2,000 soldiers died of disease at Valley Forge, Pennsylvania, but the army came out better trained.

questions.q: In 1781, the British army under Lord Cornwallis surrendered at which battle?
questions.explain: American and French forces trapped Cornwallis at Yorktown, Virginia, and his surrender in 1781 ended major fighting.

questions.q: Which country was America's most important ally in the Revolutionary War?
questions.explain: France sent money, troops and a navy, and its fleet helped trap the British at Yorktown.

questions.q: Which young French nobleman became a major general and a close friend of George Washington?
questions.explain: Lafayette joined the Continental Army at 19, served at Yorktown and remained a hero to Americans.

questions.q: Which American general became a traitor after plotting to hand West Point to the British?
questions.explain: Benedict Arnold's plot was uncovered in 1780, and he fled to the British side.

questions.q: Which Virginian declared in 1775, 'Give me liberty, or give me death!'?
questions.explain: Patrick Henry gave the famous speech to the Virginia Convention in March 1775.

questions.q: Which American spy is remembered for saying he regretted having only one life to lose for his country?
questions.explain: Nathan Hale was hanged by the British in 1776 and is reported to have said those famous last words.

questions.q: Which American naval hero is remembered for reportedly replying 'I have not yet begun to fight'?
questions.explain: John Paul Jones captured the British warship Serapis in 1779 after refusing to surrender.

questions.q: Who wrote to her husband in 1776 asking Congress to 'remember the ladies'?
questions.explain: Abigail Adams wrote to John Adams in March 1776, urging that the new laws protect women.

questions.q: During the Revolution, Benjamin Franklin served as America's diplomat in which country?
questions.explain: Franklin lived in Paris from 1776 to 1785 and helped win the French alliance.

questions.q: Phillis Wheatley, enslaved in Boston, became famous in the 1770s as what?
questions.explain: Phillis Wheatley published a book of poems in 1773, the first by an African American woman.

questions.q: What was the first written plan of government for the United States?
questions.explain: The Articles of Confederation, drafted in 1777 and ratified in 1781, created a weak national government.

questions.q: Under the Articles of Confederation, Congress could NOT do what?
questions.explain: Congress under the Articles could only ask the states for money, which left it short of funds.

questions.q: In what year was the U.S. Constitution signed?
questions.explain: Delegates signed the Constitution in Philadelphia on September 17, 1787.

questions.q: Which Virginian is called the 'Father of the Constitution'?
questions.explain: James Madison drafted the Virginia Plan and took detailed notes at the Convention.

questions.q: What is the Bill of Rights?
options: The first ten amendments to the Constitution
The opening section of the Declaration
The first article of the Constitution
The peace treaty that ended the Revolution
questions.explain: The Bill of Rights, ratified in 1791, protects freedoms such as speech, religion and trial by jury.

questions.q: The Constitution divides the government into legislative, executive and which third branch?
questions.explain: Congress makes laws, the president carries them out, and the courts, the judicial branch, interpret them.

questions.q: What is the system in which each branch of government can limit the power of the others called?
questions.explain: For example, the president can veto bills and Congress can override a veto with a two-thirds vote.

questions.q: The Preamble of the Constitution begins with which three words?
questions.explain: The Preamble opens 'We the People of the United States,' showing that power comes from the people.

questions.q: The Great Compromise of 1787 created a Congress made up of what?
questions.explain: The Senate gives each state two votes, while the House gives seats by population.

questions.q: What decides how many seats each state has in the House of Representatives?
questions.explain: House seats are shared out by population and recounted after each ten-year census.

questions.q: How many years long is a president's term under the Constitution?
questions.explain: Article II sets a four-year term for the president.

questions.q: Which essays by Hamilton, Madison and Jay urged New Yorkers to ratify the Constitution?
questions.explain: The 85 Federalist essays were published in 1787 and 1788 under the pen name Publius.

questions.q: Who were the Anti-Federalists?
questions.explain: Anti-Federalists feared a strong central government, and their demands helped produce the Bill of Rights.

questions.q: Delaware is nicknamed 'The First State' because it was the first to do what?
options: Join the Union after the Civil War
questions.explain: Delaware ratified the Constitution on December 7, 1787, before any other state.

questions.q: Who was the first president of the United States?
questions.explain: George Washington served two terms as president, from 1789 to 1797.

questions.q: Who was the first vice president of the United States?
questions.explain: John Adams served as vice president under Washington from 1789 to 1797, then became president.

questions.q: George Washington was first sworn in as president in 1789 in which city?
questions.explain: Washington took the oath on the balcony of Federal Hall in New York City on April 30, 1789.

questions.q: Which founder is often called the 'Father of His Country'?
questions.explain: Washington led the army to victory, presided over the Constitutional Convention and became the first president.

questions.q: Who was the first Secretary of the Treasury?
questions.explain: Alexander Hamilton set up the nation's finances and created the first Bank of the United States.

questions.q: What job did Thomas Jefferson hold in George Washington's first cabinet?
questions.explain: Jefferson was the first Secretary of State, from 1790 to 1793.

questions.q: What was the name of George Washington's plantation home in Virginia?
questions.explain: Mount Vernon, on the Potomac River, was Washington's home; he is buried there.

questions.q: What was the name of Thomas Jefferson's home in Virginia?
questions.explain: Jefferson designed Monticello himself; it appears on the back of the nickel.

questions.q: What was the name of George Washington's wife?
questions.explain: Martha Washington was the first First Lady, though that title came into use later.

questions.q: Who was the second president of the United States?
questions.explain: John Adams, a Federalist from Massachusetts, served one term from 1797 to 1801.

questions.q: Who was the first president to live in the White House?
questions.explain: John Adams moved into the unfinished President's House in November 1800.

questions.q: In what year did the federal government move to the new capital city of Washington?
questions.explain: Congress first met in the new Capitol in November 1800.

questions.q: In the name Washington, D.C., what do the letters 'D.C.' stand for?
questions.explain: The capital sits in the District of Columbia, a federal district that is not part of any state.

questions.q: Whose portrait appears on the one-dollar bill?
questions.explain: George Washington has appeared on the front of the $1 bill since 1869.

questions.q: Which founder, the first Secretary of the Treasury, appears on the $10 bill?
questions.explain: Alexander Hamilton has been on the $10 bill since 1929.

questions.q: Which founder's portrait appears on the $100 bill?
questions.explain: Benjamin Franklin, who was never president, has been on the $100 bill since 1914.

questions.q: Whose portrait appears on the front of the nickel?
questions.explain: Thomas Jefferson has been on the nickel since 1938, with Monticello on the back.

questions.q: Whose portrait appears on the front of the quarter?
questions.explain: George Washington has appeared on the quarter since 1932, the 200th anniversary of his birth.

questions.q: Which machine did Eli Whitney invent in 1793?
questions.explain: The cotton gin separated seeds from cotton quickly, which made cotton profitable and spread slavery.

questions.q: Alexander Hamilton led which of the first two political parties?
questions.explain: Hamilton's Federalists favored a strong national government and close ties with Britain.

questions.q: Thomas Jefferson and James Madison led which early political party?
questions.explain: Jefferson and Madison's Democratic-Republicans favored farmers, states' rights and a smaller federal government.

questions.q: The motto E Pluribus Unum, on the Great Seal since 1782, means what?
questions.explain: E Pluribus Unum is Latin for 'out of many, one,' meaning one nation made from many states.

questions.q: Which bird is at the center of the Great Seal of the United States, adopted in 1782?
questions.explain: The bald eagle on the Great Seal holds an olive branch and arrows.

questions.q: The 'Don't Tread on Me' Gadsden flag of the Revolution shows which animal?
questions.explain: The yellow Gadsden flag, designed by Christopher Gadsden, shows a coiled rattlesnake.

questions.q: Frontiersman Daniel Boone is famous for leading settlers through the Cumberland Gap into which future state?
questions.explain: In 1775 Daniel Boone blazed the Wilderness Road through the Cumberland Gap into Kentucky.

questions.q: Who was the fourth president of the United States?
questions.explain: James Madison served from 1809 to 1817 and led the nation during the War of 1812.

questions.q: About how much did the Louisiana Purchase increase the size of the United States?
questions.explain: The purchase added about 828,000 square miles, roughly doubling the size of the country.

questions.q: Which president made the Louisiana Purchase?
questions.explain: Jefferson approved the deal even though he doubted the Constitution clearly allowed it.

questions.q: Which French leader sold the Louisiana Territory to the United States?
questions.explain: Napoleon needed money for war in Europe and gave up on an empire in North America.

questions.q: Who led the 1804-1806 expedition to explore the Louisiana Purchase?
questions.explain: Jefferson sent Lewis and Clark to map the West and find a route to the Pacific.

questions.q: Which Shoshone woman served as an interpreter for the Lewis and Clark expedition?
questions.explain: Sacagawea traveled with the expedition with her infant son and helped it trade with the Shoshone for horses.

questions.q: Which ocean did Lewis and Clark reach in 1805?
questions.explain: The expedition reached the Pacific near the mouth of the Columbia River in November 1805.

questions.q: Who shot and killed Alexander Hamilton in a duel in 1804?
questions.explain: Vice President Aaron Burr shot Hamilton in a duel at Weehawken, New Jersey, in July 1804.

questions.q: The 1803 Supreme Court case Marbury v. Madison gave courts what power?
options: To declare war on other nations
To choose the president in a tie
questions.explain: Chief Justice John Marshall's ruling established judicial review, the power to void laws that break the Constitution.

questions.q: Who was president during the War of 1812?
questions.explain: Congress declared war on Britain in June 1812 at James Madison's request.

questions.q: The War of 1812 was fought between the United States and which country?
questions.explain: Americans fought Britain over the seizing of sailors, trade limits and British support for Native resistance.

questions.q: In August 1814, British troops burned which buildings in Washington?
options: The White House and the Capitol
questions.explain: British troops set fire to the President's House, the Capitol and other public buildings on August 24, 1814.

questions.q: Which First Lady saved a portrait of George Washington before the British burned the White House?
questions.explain: Dolley Madison made sure a large portrait of Washington was saved before fleeing the city in 1814.

questions.q: Who wrote the words to 'The Star-Spangled Banner' in 1814?
questions.explain: Francis Scott Key, a lawyer, wrote the poem after watching the bombardment of a fort in Baltimore.

questions.q: The British bombardment that inspired 'The Star-Spangled Banner' was aimed at which fort?
questions.explain: When the U.S. flag still flew over Fort McHenry after the 1814 attack, Key was inspired to write his poem.

questions.q: Fort McHenry, whose 1814 defense inspired the national anthem, guards the harbor of which city?
questions.explain: Fort McHenry held off British ships in Baltimore Harbor in September 1814.

questions.q: Francis Scott Key's 1814 poem became which song, made the national anthem in 1931?
questions.explain: The Star-Spangled Banner, sung to an older tune, became the national anthem by law in 1931; its flag is at the American History Museum.

questions.q: In the War of 1812, the warship USS Constitution earned what nickname?
questions.explain: British cannonballs seemed to bounce off its thick oak sides, so sailors called it Old Ironsides.

questions.q: What was Andrew Jackson's nickname?
questions.explain: Jackson's soldiers called him Old Hickory because he was as tough as hickory wood.

questions.q: The Monroe Doctrine of 1823 warned European nations against what?
questions.explain: President James Monroe declared that the Americas were closed to new European colonization.

questions.q: The Erie Canal, opened in 1825, linked New York City by water to what?
questions.explain: The canal ran from the Hudson River to Lake Erie and made New York City a trade giant.

questions.q: John Quincy Adams, the sixth president, was the son of which earlier president?
questions.explain: John Quincy Adams served from 1825 to 1829, the first son of a president to become president.

questions.q: Andrew Jackson's supporters formed which party, still active today?
questions.explain: The Democratic Party grew out of Jackson's movement in the 1820s and is the oldest active U.S. party.

questions.q: Andrew Jackson's practice of giving government jobs to loyal supporters was called what?
questions.explain: The name came from the saying 'to the victor belong the spoils.'

questions.q: The Indian Removal Act of 1830 forced Native nations to move to land in which direction?
questions.explain: Andrew Jackson signed the act, which led to the forced removal of the Cherokee, Creek, Choctaw, Chickasaw and Seminole.

questions.q: The Cherokee were forced to move to Indian Territory, in what is now which state?
questions.explain: Indian Territory covered much of present-day Oklahoma, which became a state in 1907.

questions.q: Which Shawnee leader tried to unite Native nations against U.S. expansion and died in battle in 1813?
questions.explain: Tecumseh allied with the British in the War of 1812 and was killed at the Battle of the Thames.

questions.q: 'Remember the Alamo!' was a battle cry in the fight for whose independence?
questions.explain: Texans shouted 'Remember the Alamo!' when they won independence from Mexico at San Jacinto in 1836.

questions.q: Which general won Texas independence at San Jacinto and became president of the Republic of Texas?
questions.explain: Sam Houston defeated Santa Anna in 1836; the city of Houston is named for him.

questions.q: Which frontiersman and former Tennessee congressman died defending the Alamo in 1836?
questions.explain: Davy Crockett served in Congress before joining the Texan fight and dying at the Alamo.

questions.q: What was 'Manifest Destiny' in the 1840s?
options: A plan to free all enslaved people at once
A treaty dividing Oregon with Britain
A law creating public schools in each state
The idea the U.S. should spread across the continent
questions.explain: Journalist John O'Sullivan coined the phrase in 1845 to argue for westward expansion.

questions.q: Pioneers heading west on the Oregon Trail in the 1840s mostly traveled in what?
questions.explain: Families packed covered wagons pulled by oxen for the roughly 2,000-mile trip to Oregon.

questions.q: Which war added California and much of the Southwest to the United States?
questions.explain: The 1848 Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo ended the Mexican-American War and gave the U.S. California and the Southwest.

questions.q: In 1848, the discovery of gold at Sutter's Mill set off a gold rush in what is now which state?
questions.explain: News of gold in California drew about 300,000 fortune seekers by the mid-1850s, with the first big wave, the '49ers, in 1849.

questions.q: Samuel Morse is famous for developing which invention in the 1830s and 1840s?
questions.explain: Morse sent the message 'What hath God wrought' from Washington to Baltimore in 1844.

questions.q: Robert Fulton is famous for building which early success in 1807?
questions.explain: Fulton's steamboat, the Clermont, carried passengers up the Hudson River in 1807.

questions.q: After escaping slavery in 1838, Frederick Douglass became famous as what?
questions.explain: Douglass published his life story in 1845 and became one of the most powerful voices against slavery.

questions.q: What was the secret network that helped enslaved people escape to freedom in the North called?
questions.explain: The Underground Railroad was a network of hidden routes and safe houses run by free Black people and white allies.

questions.q: What is Nat Turner known for doing in 1831?
options: Leading a revolt of enslaved people
questions.explain: Nat Turner led a revolt in Southampton County, Virginia, in 1831; Southern states then passed harsher slave laws.
